## The idea first

Adaptive dynamics asks a simple question: if a new strategy appears at very low
frequency, can it increase in the environment created by the strategies already
present? The established strategies are called **residents** and the new
strategy is called a **mutant**. Because the mutant is rare, we assume it
experiences the residents' competitive environment without noticeably changing
that environment itself.

The calculation follows one mutant seed across all the patch ages at which it
might arrive. In each possible patch, the seed may establish, grow, survive, and
produce dispersing offspring. Averaging that lifetime return across the
landscape gives a reproduction ratio: above one the mutant can invade, below
one it cannot, and at one it exactly replaces itself. The equations below use
the canopy-light environment developed on the [size-structured
PDE](size-structured-pde.qmd) page. The fitness calculation follows
@Falster-2015.

## Invasion fitness {#sec-invasion-fitness}

Let $x$ denote the traits of the resident community and $x^\prime$ the traits
of a rare mutant. We focus on phenotype-dependent fitness: the combined
consequences of those traits for growth, fecundity, and mortality in the
non-linear competitive environment created by the residents. We do not model
the genetic basis of trait inheritance or expression. Following the standard
rare-mutant assumption, the mutant has a negligible effect on the competitive
environment—in this formulation, the canopy-light profile—in which it grows
[@Geritz-1998].

In general, invasion fitness is the long-term per-capita growth rate of a rare
mutant in the environment determined by the residents [@Metz-1992]. That rate
is difficult to calculate directly in a structured metacommunity because plants
differ in size and occupy patches of different ages
[@Gyllenberg-2001; @Metz-2001].

At demographic equilibrium, we can instead use the **basic reproduction
ratio**: the expected number of new dispersers ultimately produced by one
dispersing seed. This ratio gives the same evolutionary ordering as the
long-term per-capita growth rate, so it can be used to decide whether a mutant
invades [@Gyllenberg-2001; @Metz-2001].

We denote by $R\left(x^\prime, x\right)$ the mutant's basic reproduction ratio
in the competitive environment created by residents $x$. Patches of age
$a$ have frequency-density $P(a)$ in the landscape, as derived on the
[size-structured PDE](size-structured-pde.qmd) page. More precisely, the
probability that a randomly dispersed seed lands in a patch with age in a small
interval $\mathrm{d}a$ is $P(a)\mathrm{d}a$.

The mutant may therefore land in a young, open patch or an old, shaded one. Its
overall reproduction ratio averages its return over all those possible arrival
ages $a_0$:


$$
R\left(x^\prime,x\right) = \int _0^{a_{\rm max}} P\left(a_0\right) \, S_{\rm D} \, \tilde{R}\left(x^\prime, a_0, a_{\rm max} \right) \, {\rm d}a_0
$$ {#eq-invfit}

Here $\tilde{R}\left(x^\prime, a_0, a \right)$ is the expected number of
offspring produced by one mutant seed that arrives when the patch is age $a_0$,
counted up to patch age $a$ [@Gyllenberg-2001; @Metz-2001], and $S_{\rm D}$ is
the fraction of those offspring that survive dispersal. In theory both
integrals run to infinity, so that the entire remaining lifetime of the patch
is included.
`plant` stops both integrals at $a_{\rm max}$, the patch age at which a run
ends. By default $a_{\rm max}$ is the age by which all but a small fraction of
patches have been disturbed (see the [Weibull
distribution](size-structured-pde.qmd#sec-weibull-distribution)).

That lifetime return is itself another integral. It is written here for a plant
with traits $x$; the mutant's return is the same with $x = x^\prime$ and
$a = a_{\rm max}$:


$$
\tilde{R}(x, a_0, a) = \int_{a_0}^{a} f(x, H(x, a_0, a^\prime), E_{a^\prime}) \, S_{\rm I} (x, a_0, a^\prime) \, S_{\rm P} (a_0, a^\prime) \, {\rm d} a^\prime
$$ {#eq-tilder}

The integrand is a product of three pieces:

- $f$ is the plant's fecundity at its current height and light environment;
- $S_{\rm I}$ is the probability that the plant is still alive; and
- $S_{\rm P}$ is the probability that the patch has not yet been disturbed.

The individual and patch survival probabilities are defined on the
[size-structured PDE](size-structured-pde.qmd) page. Multiplying the three terms
gives expected offspring production at patch age $a^\prime$; integrating from
arrival age $a_0$ onward gives the seed's expected lifetime return. The
fraction $S_{\rm D}$ that survives dispersal is applied once, to that total, in
@eq-invfit.

### Reading the result

The threshold is replacement:

- $R(x^\prime, x) > 1$: one mutant seed produces more than one dispersing seed
  on average, so the mutant can invade;
- $R(x^\prime, x) < 1$: it fails to replace itself and cannot invade; and
- $R(x^\prime, x) = 1$: it exactly replaces itself in that resident
  environment.

Repeating this calculation across mutant trait values gives an invasion-fitness
landscape. A resident that cannot be invaded by nearby alternatives is
evolutionarily stable. That is distinct from convergence stability: a trait can
be approached by gradual evolution yet still be invasible once reached, in
which case it can be an evolutionary branching point rather than an endpoint.
The [adaptive-dynamics examples](adaptive-dynamics/index.qmd) show both kinds of
outcome.
